newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian long bonds surge to best since Feb 94.
newsitem.headline: Australian long bonds surge to best since Feb 94.

text.p: *Australian bonds rally on late buying, with 10 year yield closing at lowest since February 23, 1994.
*Yield curve continues to flatten as long end leads the way.
*Market now waiting on U.S. payrolls later on Thursday.

A late buying surge saw Australian bonds rally strongly, despite some disappointment that the RBA had not cut rates earlier in the day, with the 10-year bond yield posting its lowest close since February 23 1994.

The market had a choppy opening session ahead of the 9.30 a.m. announcement time of any RBA move. When there was no news from the central bank, bonds had eased slightly, but quickly regained ground and strengthened on ongoing hopes for a cut.
A ratings outlook upgrade for four Australian states and some afternoon offshore futures buying, which has occurred throughout the week, helped take the market to its highs.

Following Wednesday's upgrading of Australia's credit rating outlook, Moody's Investor Services lifted the ratings outlooks of New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland and Western Australia from improving to stable.

That news buoyed the semi-government market, which flowed through to government bonds. However, traders said that at current levels there may be some profit-taking, especially if there were any doubts over the likelihood of a rate cut.
"I wouldn't be surprised if you see people selling tomorrow, taking a bit of profit. People are going to start weighing it up, whether there is the risk/reward there," one trader said.

The easing sentiment was helped by the release of the National Australia Bank June quarter business survey showing subdued conditions and contained wage and inflation pressures. NAB said they were expecting a rate cut in the next month.
"People are still looking for a rate cut, it's just the timing of it," the trader said.
Possible timings of a cut are after employment data next week, wages and inflation data later in July or after the August 5 board meeting, with the latter two the most favoured.
However, some felt the market had overpriced the chances of a cut, having been caught out badly by previous rate cuts.

"The short end is at these lofty levels not out of confidence of another easing, but out of fear of missiong another one," Bankers Trust interest rate strategist Rory Robertson said, adding he did not expect a cut until after the next RBA meeting, and even then it was only a 50/50 chance.
In the immediate future, however, the focus of the market was the U.S. June payrolls data later on Thursday.
Economists expect the data, brought forward because the U.S is closed on Friday for Independence Day, is expected to show a 222,000 rise in employment and a steady 4.8 percent unemployment rate.

Late rally sees spreads narrow across the board, with the 50 point spread to U.S. 10-years expected to provide solid resistance. NZ yields rose after RBNZ Governor Don Brash said market conditions were too easy. Curve continues to flatten, although short end caught up some ground late in the day.
